"BenchmarkTools t it %1.3e s, T eff %1.2f GB s
", t it, T eff return end iteration loop t tic Base.time niter timed 0 for iter 1 niter start the timer after 10 warm up iterations if iter 11 CUDA.synchronize t tic Base.time niter timed 0 end niter timed 1 update solution α 0.99 1 β cuda threads nthreads blocks nblocks update u u, d, α compute residual cuda threads nthreads blocks nblocks compute q qx, u, λ, dx cuda threads nthreads blocks nblocks compute r r, qx, dx check convergence if do check && iter % nchck 0 err maximum abs, r push itr h, iter nx push res h, err if err εtol println " solver converged in iter nx × N iterations 🚀" break end end save old z if iter % ndrel 0 . z0 z end compute preconditioned residual cuda threads nthreads blocks nblocks precondition z, r, Q update β if iter % ndrel 0 β compute β d, z, z0 end update search direction cuda threads nthreads blocks nblocks update d d, z, β end performance CUDA.synchronize t toc Base.time t tic t it t toc niter timed execution time per iteration s T eff A eff t it effective memory throughput GB s printf "Time %1.3f s, T eff %1.2f GB s niter %d 
", t toc, T eff, niter timed create plot if do visu fig Figure size 600, 450 ax Axis fig 1,1 xlabel "x", ylabel "u", title "solution" , Axis fig 2,1 xlabel "iter nx", ylabel "|r|", yscale log10, title "convergence history", limits 0, niter nx, 0.1εtol, 1e2 plt lines ax 1 , xc, Array u color red , lines ax 2 , itr h, res h color black return fig end return end fig elliptic 1d dr save "elliptic 1d dr gpu.png", fig elliptic 1d dr nx 2^26, niter 110, do check false, do visu false elliptic 1d dr nx 2^26, do check false, do visu false, do bench true ``` """ md""" note "Comparing GPU and CPU results" The GPU and the CPU solvers compute the same solution, but not exactly the reductions in `compute β` and in the convergence check sum the numbers in a different order on the GPU, which changes the rounding errors. As in the reference tests of lecture 4, compare the results approximately, with `≈`. On a GH200, we measured for `nx 2^26` in GB s | Version | ``T \mathrm eff `` | | | | | `elliptic 1d dr gpu.jl`, manual timer | 1478 | | `elliptic 1d dr gpu.jl`, ` belapsed compute ... ` | 1544 | | `copyto `, `n 2^28` ``T \mathrm peak `` | 3605 | That's about 23 times faster than the multi threaded solver on the M2 Max laptop from lecture 4 64 GB s . Yet, ``T \mathrm eff `` is only about 43 % of ``T \mathrm peak ``. """ md""" Kernel fusion Let's count the arrays that the kernels read and write in main memory in every iteration. As in lecture 4, we count every array once per kernel neighbouring elements, such as `u ix ` and `u ix 1 `, are loaded together from main memory. | Kernel | Reads | Writes | Arrays | | | | | | | `update u ` | `u`, `d` | `u` | 3 | | `compute q ` | `u`, `λ` | `qx` | 3 | | `compute r ` | `qx` | `r` | 2 | | `precondition ` | `Q`, `r` | `z` | 3 | | `update d ` | `d`, `z` | `d` | 3 | | total | | | 14 | The effective memory access ``A \mathrm eff `` only counts 6 arrays the unknown fields `u` and `d` are read and written, and the known fields `λ` and `Q` are read. Therefore, ``T \mathrm eff `` can reach at most 6 14 ≈ 43% of ``T \mathrm peak ``. Kernel fusion merges several kernels into one, to avoid storing intermediate results in main memory. The flux `qx` doesn't depend on its own history instead of storing it, we can recompute it on the fly in the kernel that computes the residual. The thread `ix` needs the fluxes on both sides of the grid point `ix 1` ```julia function compute r r, u, λ, dx ix blockIdx .x 1 blockDim .x threadIdx .x if ix length r inbounds begin qxW λ ix u ix 1 u ix dx qxE λ ix 1 u ix 2 u ix 1 dx r ix qxE qxW dx end end return end ``` Every flux is now computed twice, by two neighbouring threads, but floating point operations are "for free" in memory bound codes. The fused kernel reads `u` and `λ`, and writes `r` 3 arrays instead of 5, i.e. 12 arrays per iteration, and an upper bound of 6 12 50% of ``T \mathrm peak ``. 👉 Duplicate `elliptic 1d dr gpu.jl`, rename the copy to `elliptic 1d dr gpu fused.jl`, replace `compute q ` and `compute r ` with the fused kernel, and remove the array `qx`. Check that the solver still converges, and measure ``T \mathrm eff `` for `nx 2^26`. On a GH200, we measured ``T \mathrm eff `` 1737 GB s with the manual timer, and 1830 GB s with ` belapsed`, i.e. about 50 % of ``T \mathrm peak ``. Both versions of the solver reach the upper bound given by the number of arrays that they read and write. Why not fuse all kernels into one? The residual at the grid point `ix 1` depends on the updated values of `u` at the neighbouring points, which are computed by other threads, possibly in other blocks. Kernels that need results of other threads can't be fused they need the synchronisation between two kernel launches. On the other hand, `precondition ` only uses the residual at the same grid point, and could be fused with `compute r `. """ md""" Data races The threads of a kernel run concurrently, in an unspecified order. A data race occurs if a thread reads a memory location that another thread of the same kernel writes, or if two threads write to the same location the result then depends on the execution order of the threads. Consider three kernels with the index `ix` of an inner grid point ```julia A ix 2 A ix ✅ every thread reads and writes only its own element B ix A ix 1 2 A ix A ix 1 ✅ A is only read, B is only written A ix A ix 1 2 A ix A ix 1 ❌ data race A ix 1 and A ix 1 may be already updated ``` To update a stencil, write the new values to a second array, and swap the two arrays after the kernel ```julia cuda threads nthreads blocks nblocks update A2, A A, A2 A2, A swaps the names of the arrays, without copying them ``` In our DR solver, `update u ` writes `u`, but every thread reads only its own element `u ix 1 `, and `compute q ` reads the neighbouring values of `u`, but writes `qx` there is no data race. note "Array programming and aliasing" With array programming, the in place update ` . A 2 end 1 A 1 end 2 2 A 2 end 1 A 3 end ` is correct Julia detects that the arrays on both sides of the assignment overlap, and makes a temporary copy of the right hand side. In kernels, avoiding data races is our responsibility. To see what can happen, let's emulate a kernel on the CPU, executing the "threads" one after another, in different orders. The function `smooth ` writes the result to a second array, the function `smooth inplace ` updates the array in place """ function smooth B, A, order for ix in order B ix A ix 1 A ix A ix 1 3 end return B end function smooth inplace A, order for ix in order A ix A ix 1 A ix A ix 1 3 end return A end let A0 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 3.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 inner 2 length A0 1 orders collect inner , collect reverse inner , shuffle Xoshiro 1 , inner rows "| order of the threads | `smooth ` | `smooth inplace ` |", "| | | |" for order in orders B smooth copy A0 , A0, order A smooth inplace copy A0 , order push rows, "| ` order` | ` round. B digits 2 ` | ` round. A digits 2 ` |" end Markdown.parse join rows, "
" end md""" With a second array, the result doesn't depend on the order of the threads. In place, every order gives a different result. On a GPU, the order changes from run to run, and the results of a kernel with a data race are not reproducible. """ md""" Wrapping up GPUs hide the memory latency by running many threads. In the CUDA programming model, the threads are grouped into blocks, which form the grid. Blocks and grid can be 1D, 2D or 3D, and every thread computes its global indices from `threadIdx `, `blockIdx ` and `blockDim `. On a supercomputer, we compute on compute nodes requested from SLURM, not on the login nodes. With CUDA.jl, array programming codes run on GPUs with few changes. Kernel programming gives full control over the computations of every thread. Kernel launches are asynchronous synchronise before measuring the time. We ported the DR solver to the GPU. Kernel fusion reduces the number of arrays accessed in main memory, and increases ``T \mathrm eff ``. A data race occurs when a thread reads or writes memory that another thread of the same kernel writes. Write the results of stencil updates to a second array. """

title: xPU computing
text:
xPU computingThe goal of this lecture is to become familiar with:Backend-portable (xPU) programming with ParallelStencil.jl: a single code that runs on both CPUs and GPUs.Stencil computations with math-close notation (@parallel) and with explicit kernel programming (@parallel_indices).Solving the elliptic problem in 2D and 3D with dynamic relaxation (DR).Unit and reference tests of a Julia package, and continuous integration (CI) with GitHub Actions.In lecture 4, we parallelised the DR solver for the steady diffusion equation on the CPU with multi-threading, and in lecture 5, we ported it to the GPU with CUDA.jl. We now have two versions of the same solver, which we have to maintain separately. As we saw in lecture 1, Julia solves the two-language problem: the same high-level language serves for prototyping and for high-performance production codes. With the ParallelStencil.jl package, we can go one step further and write a single code that runs on both CPUs and GPUs, which we call an xPU code. We can then prototype and debug on the CPU of a laptop, and switch to GPUs for production runs.In this lecture, we will merge our CPU and GPU solvers into a single xPU code, and extend it to 2D and 3D. Finally, we will learn how to test a solver automatically on GitHub.Backend-portable xPU programmingParallelStencil.jl enables writing architecture-agnostic, high-level code for high-performance stencil computations on CPUs and GPUs. It relies on the native kernel programming capabilities of:CUDA.jl for Nvidia GPUs;AMDGPU.jl for AMD GPUs;Metal.jl for Apple GPUs;Base.Threads and Polyester.jl for multi-threaded CPUs.👉 Take a quick tour of ParallelStencil’s README. Then, on your computer and on daint, create a folder for this lecture, make it a Julia project, and add the packages ParallelStencil, AcceleratedKernels, BenchmarkTools and CairoMakie, as well as CUDA on daint.InitialisationParallelStencil is initialised with the macro @init_parallel_stencil, which takes the package used for parallelisation (the backend), the number type, and the number of dimensions. A boolean constant USE_GPU lets us select the backend:const USE_GPU = false
@static if USE_GPU
    using CUDA
end
using ParallelStencil
using ParallelStencil.FiniteDifferences2D
@static if USE_GPU
    @init_parallel_stencil(CUDA, Float64, 2, inbounds=false)
else
    @init_parallel_stencil(Threads, Float64, 2, inbounds=false)
end
The backend package, here CUDA, must be loaded before ParallelStencil. @static if evaluates the condition when the code is parsed: with USE_GPU = false, CUDA is never loaded, and the code also runs on computers without an Nvidia GPU.With the Threads backend, the kernels run on the CPU with multi-threading: start Julia with several threads, e.g. julia --project -t auto, as in lecture 4.With inbounds=false, Julia checks the array bounds in all kernels. Once your code produces the expected results, you can set inbounds=true to deactivate the bounds checks, which may improve the performance.Restart Julia after changing the backendParallelStencil can only be initialised once per Julia session. Restart Julia after changing USE_GPU.@init_parallel_stencil creates the module Data. Data.Array is the array type of the selected backend and number type: Array{Float64} with the Threads backend, and CuArray{Float64} with the CUDA backend. ParallelStencil also provides macros that allocate arrays of this type:A = @zeros(nx, ny)           # array of zeros, on the CPU or on the GPU
B = @ones(nx, ny)            # array of ones
C = @rand(nx, ny)            # array of random numbers
D = Data.Array(rand(nx, ny)) # copy an array from the CPU to the backend
d = Array(D)                 # copy an array from the backend to the CPU, e.g. for plotting
Other backendsOn Apple computers, the Metal backend runs the kernels on the integrated GPU. However, Apple GPUs don’t support Float64 numbers, so we don’t use the Metal backend in this course.ParallelStencil also provides a KernelAbstractions backend, which switches between CPUs and GPUs at runtime, without restarting Julia (see Interactive prototyping with runtime hardware selection in the README).Two ways to write kernelsParallelStencil supports two ways of writing kernels:Stencil computations with math-close notation: kernels declared with @parallel are written with macros, e.g. from the submodule ParallelStencil.FiniteDifferences2D, which compute finite differences of whole arrays, without explicit indices. The notation is close to the array programming notation of lectures 2 and 3.Explicit kernel programming: kernels declared with @parallel_indices work with explicit indices, like the CUDA kernels of lecture 5.Both kinds of kernels are launched with @parallel:@parallel kernel!(args...)
ParallelStencil computes the launch parameters, i.e. the number of threads per block and the number of blocks, automatically. In contrast to @cuda, @parallel waits until the kernel has completed. Therefore, we don’t need to synchronise before reading the timer.Math-close notationThe submodule FiniteDifferences2D provides macros to select array elements, and to compute differences and averages of neighbouring array elements. The suffix a stands for “all”: the macro operates on all elements in the other dimension. The suffix i stands for “inner”: the macro selects the inner elements in the other dimension. For an array A of size nx × ny:MacroArray programming equivalentSize@all(A)Anx × ny@inn(A)A[2:end-1, 2:end-1](nx-2) × (ny-2)@d_xa(A)A[2:end, :] - A[1:end-1, :](nx-1) × ny@d_ya(A)A[:, 2:end] - A[:, 1:end-1]nx × (ny-1)@d_xi(A)A[2:end, 2:end-1] - A[1:end-1, 2:end-1](nx-1) × (ny-2)@d_yi(A)A[2:end-1, 2:end] - A[2:end-1, 1:end-1](nx-2) × (ny-1)@av_xi(A)(A[1:end-1, 2:end-1] + A[2:end, 2:end-1]) / 2(nx-1) × (ny-2)@av_yi(A)(A[2:end-1, 1:end-1] + A[2:end-1, 2:end]) / 2(nx-2) × (ny-1)Type ?FiniteDifferences2D in the REPL to list all macros, e.g. for harmonic averages (@harm_xi) and second-order differences (@d2_xi), and ?@d_xi to read the documentation of a macro:julia> using ParallelStencil.FiniteDifferences2D

help?> @d_xi
  @d_xi(A): Compute differences between adjacent elements of A along the dimension x and select the inner elements of A in the remaining dimension. Corresponds to @inn_y(@d_xa(A)).
A @parallel kernel consists of assignments to arrays written with these macros, and returns nothing. For example, the update of the solution @. u[2:end-1, 2:end-1] += α * d becomes:@parallel function update_u!(u, d, α)
    @inn(u) = @inn(u) + α * @all(d)
    return
end
All the terms of a statement must have the same size, here (nx-2) × (ny-2). However, a kernel can contain several statements that operate on arrays of different sizes: each statement is only computed for the indices within the bounds of the array on its left-hand side.WarningUpdate operators, such as += and -=, are not supported in @parallel kernels: write out the assignment, as in the example above.How does it work?@parallel turns the kernel into a kernel with explicit indices, similar to the kernels that you wrote in lecture 5, together with the code that launches it on the selected backend. This is possible thanks to Julia’s metaprogramming capabilities. Feel free to explore the source code!The elliptic problem in 2DWe solve the steady diffusion equation from lectures 3–5 in the 2D domain \([0, l_x] \times [0, l_y]\):\[\boldsymbol{\nabla}\cdot(\lambda \boldsymbol{\nabla} u) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\lambda \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\lambda \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) = 0~.\]As in 1D, we compute the residual from the diffusive flux \(\boldsymbol{q} = -\lambda \boldsymbol{\nabla} u\), which now has two components:\[q_x = -\lambda \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}~, \qquad q_y = -\lambda \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}~, \qquad r = -\left(\frac{\partial q_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial q_y}{\partial y}\right)~.\]The DR iterations, i.e. the updates of the solution \(u\), of the preconditioned residual \(z\), of the search direction \(d\) and of the damping parameter \(\beta\), remain unchanged.DiscretisationWe extend the staggered grid from lecture 3 to 2D:The solution u is defined at the cell centres (xc, yc), and has nx × ny elements. The values in the first and last rows and columns are prescribed by the boundary conditions, and the (nx-2) × (ny-2) inner values are the unknowns.The flux qx is located on the cell faces between the cell centres in the x direction, and has (nx-1) × (ny-2) elements. The flux qy is located on the cell faces in the y direction, and has (nx-2) × (ny-1) elements. We only need the fluxes across the faces of the inner cells.The residual r, the preconditioned residuals z and z0, the search direction d and the preconditioner Q are defined at the inner cell centres, and have (nx-2) × (ny-2) elements.In 1D, the diffusion coefficient λ is defined at the same locations as the flux qx. In 2D, we need λ at the locations of both flux components. Instead of storing λ twice, in arrays of the sizes of qx and qy, we define it once at the cell centres, like u, with nx × ny elements. We then compute the values of λ at the cell faces as the averages of the values in the two neighbouring cells. Compared to two (or, in 3D, three) arrays, this reduces the memory footprint of the solver. We sample λ from a Gaussian anomaly in the centre of the domain:\[\lambda(x, y) = \lambda_\mathrm{bg} + \lambda_\mathrm{amp} \exp\left(-(x - l_x/2)^2 - (y - l_y/2)^2\right)~.\]As in 1D, we impose \(u = 0\) at \(x = 0\) and \(u = 1\) at \(x = l_x\). At the boundaries \(y = 0\) and \(y = l_y\), we prescribe the linear profile between these two values, which is the solution for a constant \(\lambda\). Far from the anomaly, the solution is close to this profile.Preconditioner👉 Write down the discretised residual at an inner grid cell, and derive the Jacobi preconditioner Q as in lecture 3: collect the coefficient of the value of u at that cell, negate it, and take its inverse.Want to see the answer?AnswerThe element r[ix, iy] is located at the cell centre of u[ix+1, iy+1]. With the fluxes across the four faces of this cell, the discretised residual reads:r[ix, iy] = -((qx[ix+1, iy] - qx[ix, iy]) / dx + (qy[ix, iy+1] - qy[ix, iy]) / dy)
qx[ix, iy] = -0.5 * (λ[ix, iy+1] + λ[ix+1, iy+1]) * (u[ix+1, iy+1] - u[ix, iy+1]) / dx
qy[ix, iy] = -0.5 * (λ[ix+1, iy] + λ[ix+1, iy+1]) * (u[ix+1, iy+1] - u[ix+1, iy]) / dy
The coefficient of u[ix+1, iy+1] in r[ix, iy] is:-0.5 * (λ[ix, iy+1] + 2λ[ix+1, iy+1] + λ[ix+2, iy+1]) / dx^2 - 0.5 * (λ[ix+1, iy] + 2λ[ix+1, iy+1] + λ[ix+1, iy+2]) / dy^2
Therefore, the preconditioner is:λc   = λ[2:end-1, 2:end-1]
Q    = @. 2.0 / ((λ[1:end-2, 2:end-1] + 2.0 * λc + λ[3:end, 2:end-1]) * _dx^2 +
                 (λ[2:end-1, 1:end-2] + 2.0 * λc + λ[2:end-1, 3:end]) * _dy^2)
The terms in parentheses, divided by 2, are the sums of the values of λ on the two faces of the cell in each direction, as in the 1D formula Q = dx^2 / (λ[1:end-1] + λ[2:end]) from lecture 3. The array λc is a view of the inner values of λ, since the solver function is annotated with @views.Iteration parameters and performance metricWe keep the initial value of the damping parameter from 1D, using the largest number of grid cells: β = 1 - 2π / max(nx, ny). The DR solver then adapts β during the iterations.We use the same number of grid cells in both directions, ny = nx. As in 1D, the number of iterations needed to converge scales with nx, so we keep normalising the iteration count by nx.The unknown fields are u and d, and the known fields are λ and Q. Assuming that all arrays have nx × ny elements, the effective memory access per iteration is:A_eff = (2*2 + 2) * nx * ny * sizeof(Float64) / 1e9 # [GB]
A 2D xPU solver with math-close notation👉 Duplicate the script elliptic_1d_dr_gpu.jl from lecture 5, rename the copy to elliptic_2d_dr_xpu.jl, and follow the steps below.1. PackagesReplace using CUDA with the initialisation of ParallelStencil shown above, and add using AcceleratedKernels. Remove the macro @d_xa that we defined in lecture 4: FiniteDifferences2D provides its own version of it.2. Preprocessing and array initialisationRename the function to elliptic_2d_dr, set the default resolution to nx=128, and add the keyword argument ny=nx. Extend the # physics and # preprocessing sections to 2D, and initialise the arrays on the backend with Data.Array and @zeros:# physics
lx, ly = 20.0, 20.0
λbg    = 1.0
λamp   = 10.0
...
# preprocessing
dx, dy = lx / nx, ly / ny
xc, yc = LinRange(dx/2, lx-dx/2, nx), LinRange(dy/2, ly-dy/2, ny)
β      = 1 - 2π / max(nx, ny)
_dx, _dy = 1.0 / dx, 1.0 / dy
# array initialisation
u    = Data.Array([(x - xc[1]) / (xc[end] - xc[1]) for x in xc, y in yc])
u[2:end-1, 2:end-1] .= 0.0
λ    = Data.Array([λbg + λamp * exp(-(x - lx/2)^2 - (y - ly/2)^2) for x in xc, y in yc])
qx   = @zeros(nx-1, ny-2)
qy   = @zeros(nx-2, ny-1)
d    = @zeros(nx-2, ny-2)
...
The array comprehensions [... for x in xc, y in yc] create 2D arrays on the CPU, which Data.Array copies to the backend. We first initialise u with the linear profile, which sets the boundary values, and then set its inner values, our initial guess, to zero.👉 Complete the array initialisation, and compute the preconditioner Q derived above. Since Q is computed by broadcasting from λ, it ends up on the backend without changes. Finally, remove the boundary conditions before the iteration loop: the initialisation of u already sets the boundary values, which never change, since update_u! only updates the inner values.3. KernelsReplace the CUDA kernels with @parallel kernels. The kernel update_u! is given above.👉 Implement the kernels compute_q!(qx, qy, u, λ, _dx, _dy), compute_r!(r, qx, qy, _dx, _dy), precondition!(z, r, Q) and update_d!(d, z, β).HintCheck the sizes: @av_xi(λ) and @d_xi(u) have the same size as qx, and @d_xa(qx) has the same size as r.As in lecture 5, the fluxes and the residual must be computed in separate kernels: the residual of a cell depends on fluxes computed by other threads.Want to see the answer?Answer@parallel function compute_q!(qx, qy, u, λ, _dx, _dy)
    @all(qx) = -@av_xi(λ) * @d_xi(u) * _dx
    @all(qy) = -@av_yi(λ) * @d_yi(u) * _dy
    return
end

@parallel function compute_r!(r, qx, qy, _dx, _dy)
    @all(r) = -(@d_xa(qx) * _dx + @d_ya(qy) * _dy)
    return
end

@parallel function precondition!(z, r, Q)
    @all(z) = @all(Q) * @all(r)
    return
end

@parallel function update_d!(d, z, β)
    @all(d) = @all(d) * β + @all(z)
    return
end
4. The \(\beta\) update👉 Copy the function compute_β from lecture 4, which computes the dot products with AcceleratedKernels.mapreduce. AcceleratedKernels.jl is backend-agnostic, like ParallelStencil: the reductions run multi-threaded for CPU arrays, and on the GPU for GPU arrays. The convergence check with maximum(abs, r) and saving z to z0 with broadcasting work on both backends without changes.5. Iteration loop and benchmarking👉 Launch the kernels with @parallel in the iteration loop and in the function compute!, e.g.:@parallel update_u!(u, d, α)
Since ParallelStencil computes the launch parameters, and @parallel waits until the kernel has completed:remove the launch parameters nthreads and nblocks;remove CUDA.synchronize() around the timer, and CUDA.@sync in the benchmark with @belapsed.Also update the arguments of compute!, and the effective memory access A_eff.6. Visualisation👉 Replace the line plot of the solution with a heatmap, and add contour lines that show how the anomaly of λ deflects the solution. Since there is no display on the compute nodes of daint, save the figure in the solver function. Finally, return the solution, copied to the CPU, and the convergence history, e.g. for further analysis or for testing:# visualisation

    fig = Figure(size=(600, 750))

           Axis(fig[2,1]; xlabel="iter/nx", ylabel="|r|",
                          yscale=log10,

           lines!(ax[2], itr_h, res_h; color=:black))

Running the solver👉 Run the script on your computer with USE_GPU = false and several threads. With the default parameters, the solver converges in about 6.6 × nx iterations, and produces the following figure:👉 Double the resolution. Does the number of iterations, normalised by nx, stay the same?👉 On a compute node of daint, set USE_GPU = true and run the same script on the GPU, without changing anything else in the code. For the performance measurements, increase the resolution to nx = 2^13.Want to see the answer?Answerconst USE_GPU = false
@static if USE_GPU
    using CUDA
end
using ParallelStencil
using ParallelStencil.FiniteDifferences2D
@static if USE_GPU
    @init_parallel_stencil(CUDA, Float64, 2, inbounds=false)
else
    @init_parallel_stencil(Threads, Float64, 2, inbounds=false)
end
using CairoMakie
using Printf
using BenchmarkTools
using AcceleratedKernels

@parallel function update_u!(u, d, α)
    @inn(u) = @inn(u) + α * @all(d)
    return
end

@parallel function compute_q!(qx, qy, u, λ, _dx, _dy)
    @all(qx) = -@av_xi(λ) * @d_xi(u) * _dx
    @all(qy) = -@av_yi(λ) * @d_yi(u) * _dy
    return
end

@parallel function compute_r!(r, qx, qy, _dx, _dy)
    @all(r) = -(@d_xa(qx) * _dx + @d_ya(qy) * _dy)
    return
end

@parallel function precondition!(z, r, Q)
    @all(z) = @all(Q) * @all(r)
    return
end

function compute_β(d, z, z0)
    num = AcceleratedKernels.mapreduce((_d, _z, _z0) -> _d * (_z - _z0), +, d, z, z0)
    den = AcceleratedKernels.mapreduce(*, +, d, d)
    γ = abs(num) / den
    return (1 - sqrt(γ))^2
end

@parallel function update_d!(d, z, β)
    @all(d) = @all(d) * β + @all(z)
    return
end

function compute!(u, d, z, r, qx, qy, λ, Q, α, β, _dx, _dy)
    @parallel update_u!(u, d, α)
    @parallel compute_q!(qx, qy, u, λ, _dx, _dy)
    @parallel compute_r!(r, qx, qy, _dx, _dy)
    @parallel precondition!(z, r, Q)
    @parallel update_d!(d, z, β)
    return
end

@views function elliptic_2d_dr(; nx=128, ny=nx, niter=15nx, do_check=true, do_visu=true, do_bench=false)
    # physics
    lx, ly = 20.0, 20.0
    λbg    = 1.0
    λamp   = 10.0
    # numerics
    εtol  = 1e-6
    nchck = ceil(Int, 0.1nx)
    ndrel = 10
    # preprocessing
    dx, dy = lx / nx, ly / ny
    xc, yc = LinRange(dx/2, lx-dx/2, nx), LinRange(dy/2, ly-dy/2, ny)
    β      = 1 - 2π / max(nx, ny)
    _dx, _dy = 1.0 / dx, 1.0 / dy
    # array initialisation
    u    = Data.Array([(x - xc[1]) / (xc[end] - xc[1]) for x in xc, y in yc])
    u[2:end-1, 2:end-1] .= 0.0
    λ    = Data.Array([λbg + λamp * exp(-(x - lx/2)^2 - (y - ly/2)^2) for x in xc, y in yc])
    qx   = @zeros(nx-1, ny-2)
    qy   = @zeros(nx-2, ny-1)
    d    = @zeros(nx-2, ny-2)
    r    = @zeros(nx-2, ny-2)
    z    = @zeros(nx-2, ny-2)
    z0   = @zeros(nx-2, ny-2)
    # preconditioner
    λc   = λ[2:end-1, 2:end-1]
    Q    = @. 2.0 / ((λ[1:end-2, 2:end-1] + 2.0 * λc + λ[3:end, 2:end-1]) * _dx^2 +
                     (λ[2:end-1, 1:end-2] + 2.0 * λc + λ[2:end-1, 3:end]) * _dy^2)
    # convergence history
    itr_h = Float64[]
    res_h = Float64[]
    # effective main memory access per iteration [GB]
    A_eff = (2*2 + 2) * nx * ny * sizeof(Float64) / 1e9
    # benchmark one iteration with BenchmarkTools
    if do_bench
        α     = 0.99 * (1 + β)
        t_it  = @belapsed compute!($u, $d, $z, $r, $qx, $qy, $λ, $Q, $α, $β, $_dx, $_dy)
        T_eff = A_eff / t_it
        @printf("BenchmarkTools: t_it = %1.3e s, T_eff = %1.2f GB/s\n", t_it, T_eff)
        return
    end
    # iteration loop
    t_tic = Base.time(); niter_timed = 0
    for iter = 1:niter
        # start the timer after 10 warm-up iterations
        if iter == 11 t_tic = Base.time(); niter_timed = 0 end
        niter_timed += 1
        # update solution
        α = 0.99 * (1 + β)
        @parallel update_u!(u, d, α)
        # compute residual
        @parallel compute_q!(qx, qy, u, λ, _dx, _dy)
        @parallel compute_r!(r, qx, qy, _dx, _dy)
        # check convergence
        if do_check && iter % nchck == 0
            err = maximum(abs, r)
            push!(itr_h, iter / nx)
            push!(res_h, err)
            if err < εtol
                println(" solver converged in $(iter/nx) × N iterations! 🚀")
                break
            end
        end
        # save old z
        if iter % ndrel == 0
            @. z0 = z
        end
        # compute preconditioned residual
        @parallel precondition!(z, r, Q)
        # update β

    return
end

@parallel_indices (ix, iy, iz) function compute_r!(r, u, λ, _dx, _dy, _dz)
    qxW = -0.5 * (λ[ix  , iy+1, iz+1] + λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1]) * (u[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] - u[ix  , iy+1, iz+1]) * _dx
    qxE = -0.5 * (λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] + λ[ix+2, iy+1, iz+1]) * (u[ix+2, iy+1, iz+1] - u[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1]) * _dx
    qyS = -0.5 * (λ[ix+1, iy  , iz+1] + λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1]) * (u[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] - u[ix+1, iy  , iz+1]) * _dy
    qyN = -0.5 * (λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] + λ[ix+1, iy+2, iz+1]) * (u[ix+1, iy+2, iz+1] - u[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1]) * _dy
    qzB = -0.5 * (λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz  ] + λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1]) * (u[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] - u[ix+1, iy+1, iz  ]) * _dz
    qzT = -0.5 * (λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] + λ[ix+1, iy+1, iz+2]) * (u[ix+1, iy+1, iz+2] - u[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1]) * _dz
    r[ix, iy, iz] = -((qxE - qxW) * _dx + (qyN - qyS) * _dy + (qzT - qzB) * _dz)
    return
end

@parallel_indices (ix, iy, iz) function precondition!(z, r, Q)
    z[ix, iy, iz] = Q[ix, iy, iz] * r[ix, iy, iz]
    return
end

@parallel_indices (ix, iy, iz) function update_d!(d, z, β)
    d[ix, iy, iz] = d[ix, iy, iz] * β + z[ix, iy, iz]
    return
end

function compute!(u, d, z, r, λ, Q, α, β, _dx, _dy, _dz)
    nx, ny, nz = size(u)
    @parallel (1:nx-2, 1:ny-2, 1:nz-2) update_u!(u, d, α)
    @parallel (1:nx-2, 1:ny-2, 1:nz-2) compute_r!(r, u, λ, _dx, _dy, _dz)
    @parallel precondition!(z, r, Q)
    @parallel update_d!(d, z, β)
    return
end
In the function elliptic_3d_dr, remove the arrays qx, qy and qz, and launch update_u! and compute_r! with the ranges (1:nx-2, 1:ny-2, 1:nz-2).On the M2 Max laptop, with 8 threads and 256 × 256 × 256 grid cells, i.e. as many grid cells as in 2D, we measured (in GB/s):Versionmanual timer@belapsed compute!(...)elliptic_3d_dr_xpu.jl1618elliptic_3d_dr_perf_xpu.jl2739In 3D, the solver accesses 18 arrays per iteration with math-close notation, and 12 arrays with the fused residual kernel, while \(A_\mathrm{eff}\) counts 6 arrays. The upper bounds of \(T_\mathrm{eff}\), 33% and 50% of \(T_\mathrm{peak}\), are thus similar to 2D. Why is \(T_\mathrm{eff}\) lower in 3D?DiscussionOur count of the memory accesses assumes that neighbouring array elements are loaded together from main memory, and then reused from the cache. In 2D, the neighbours in the y direction are one column, i.e. nx elements, apart in memory. In 3D, the neighbours in the z direction are one xy-plane, i.e. nx × ny elements, apart. To reuse the values of an array, the cache must hold several planes of it, which is often not the case: some values are loaded from main memory several times, and the actual memory traffic is larger than our estimate. GPUs face the same challenge. Optimising 3D stencil codes for the caches and the on-chip memory is an advanced topic, which we will come back to later in this course.👉 Measure \(T_\mathrm{eff}\) of both 3D versions on a GH200 of daint with nx = 2^9, i.e. 512 × 512 × 512 grid cells.Memory usage in 3DWith 512 × 512 × 512 grid cells, every array occupies about 1.1 GB of memory. The math-close version allocates 10 arrays, i.e. about 11 GB, which fits into the 96 GB of the GH200. Keep the memory usage in mind when increasing the resolution: doubling the number of grid cells in every direction increases the memory usage by a factor of 8.Towards multi-xPUParallelStencil is seamlessly interoperable with ImplicitGlobalGrid.jl, which distributes stencil-based xPU applications on a regular staggered grid across many CPUs or GPUs, and achieves close to ideal weak scaling on thousands of GPUs. Moreover, ParallelStencil can hide the communication between GPUs behind the computations with a single macro call. This will be the topic of the next lectures.NoteHead to ParallelStencil’s miniapp section if you are curious about applications from various domain sciences implemented with ParallelStencil.Wrapping upWith ParallelStencil.jl, a single code runs on CPUs and GPUs: the backend is selected in @init_parallel_stencil, and the arrays are allocated with @zeros or copied to the backend with Data.Array.@parallel kernels with math-close notation are concise, and are easy to extend from 2D to 3D. @parallel_indices kernels give full control over the computations of every thread, e.g. for kernel fusion.We extended the DR solver to 2D and 3D: the number of iterations still scales linearly with the number of grid cells in each direction. Defining λ at the cell centres, and averaging it to the cell faces, reduces the memory footprint of the solver.Testing and continuous integrationIn lecture 4, we wrote unit tests with the Test standard library. In this part, we will put a solver into a small Julia package, test it with ] test, and run the tests automatically on GitHub after every push.Nowadays, good numerical software is expected to be well tested. The final projects of this course must therefore contain unit and reference tests, which run automatically on GitHub.Kinds of testsUnit tests check small parts of the code, usually single functions.Integration tests check larger parts of the code, e.g. a whole solver.Reference tests compare the results of the code with the results of a previous version, which we consider correct. A reference test doesn’t tell whether the results are correct, but it detects any change of the results, e.g. after optimising the code.Continuous integration (CI) runs the tests automatically whenever the code changes, e.g. on every push to GitHub.Reference tests of simulationsThe results of floating-point computations depend on the order of the operations, e.g. on the GPU or with a different number of threads. Compare the results approximately, with ≈ and a suitable tolerance. For large simulations, compare only the values at a few tens of grid points.A small packageThe command test of the package mode runs the tests of a package, which are located in the file test/runtests.jl. A package is a Julia project with a name, a unique identifier (UUID), and a module of the same name in the file src/<name>.jl.👉 Generate a package Elliptic1D on your computer, outside your course repository:julia> ]

(@v1.12) pkg> generate Elliptic1D
  Generating  project Elliptic1D:
    Elliptic1D/Project.toml
    Elliptic1D/src/Elliptic1D.jl
generate creates the folder Elliptic1D with the file Project.toml, which contains the name and the UUID of the package, and the file src/Elliptic1D.jl with the module Elliptic1D.👉 Replace the content of src/Elliptic1D.jl with the DR solver from lecture 4, without the plotting and the timing:Move the β update into a function compute_β(d, z, z0), which we can test separately.Return the solution and the convergence history.Export the function elliptic_1d_dr, so that it is available after using Elliptic1D.Then, start Julia in the package folder with julia --project, and add the dependency LinearAlgebra with ] add LinearAlgebra. Even standard libraries have to be declared as dependencies of a package.Want to see the answer?Answermodule Elliptic1D

using LinearAlgebra

export elliptic_1d_dr

# estimate the damping parameter β from the search direction d
# and the change of the preconditioned residual z - z0
function compute_β(d, z, z0)
    γ = abs(dot(d, z .- z0)) / dot(d, d)
    return (1 - sqrt(γ))^2
end

@views function elliptic_1d_dr(; nx=200, niter=15nx)
    # physics
    lx   = 20.0
    λbg  = 1.0
    λamp = 10.0
    # numerics
    εtol  = 1e-6
    nchck = ceil(Int, 0.1nx)
    ndrel = 10
    # preprocessing
    dx   = lx / nx
    xv   = LinRange(dx,lx-dx,nx-1)
    β    = 1 - 2π / nx
    # array initialisation
    u    = zeros(nx)
    λ    = @. λbg + λamp * exp(-(xv-lx/2)^2)
    qx   = zeros(nx-1)
    d    = zeros(nx-2)
    r    = zeros(nx-2)
    z    = zeros(nx-2)
    z0   = zeros(nx-2)
    # preconditioner
    Q    = @. dx^2 / (λ[1:end-1] + λ[2:end])
    # convergence history
    itr_h = Float64[]
    res_h = Float64[]
    # iteration loop
    for iter = 1:niter
        # update solution
        α = 0.99 * (1 + β)
        @. u[2:end-1] += α * d
        # boundary conditions
        u[1]   = 0
        u[end] = 1
        # compute residual
        @. qx = -λ * (u[2:end] - u[1:end-1]) / dx
        @. r  = -(qx[2:end] - qx[1:end-1]) / dx
        # check convergence
        if iter % nchck == 0
            err = maximum(abs, r)
            push!(itr_h, iter / nx)
            push!(res_h, err)
            if err < εtol
                break
            end
        end
        # save old z
        if iter % ndrel == 0
            @. z0 = z
        end
        # compute preconditioned residual
        @. z = Q * r
        # update β
        if iter % ndrel == 0
            β = compute_β(d, z, z0)
        end
        # update search direction
        @. d = d * β + z
    end
    return u, itr_h, res_h
end

end # module Elliptic1D
Writing the testsThe tests of a package run in a separate environment, which contains the package itself and the dependencies of the tests. We declare these in the file test/Project.toml.👉 Create the test environment, and add the Test standard library to it:(Elliptic1D) pkg> activate test

(test) pkg> add Test

(test) pkg> activate .
👉 Create the file test/runtests.jl, which loads the packages Elliptic1D and Test, and contains:unit tests of the function compute_β: if z doesn’t change, then \(\gamma = 0\) and \(\beta = 1\); if z changes by d, then \(\gamma = 1\) and \(\beta = 0\);a reference test: run the solver with nx = 64, check that it converges, and compare the solution at a few grid points with reference values, which you obtain from a run of your current solver.Functions that are not exported, such as compute_β, are accessed with the module name: Elliptic1D.compute_β.Want to see the answer?Answerusing Elliptic1D
using Test

@testset "Elliptic1D" begin
    @testset "unit tests: compute_β" begin
        d  = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
        z0 = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]
        # z doesn't change: γ = 0, no damping
        @test Elliptic1D.compute_β(d, z0, z0) == 1.0
        # z changes by d: γ = 1, full damping
        @test Elliptic1D.compute_β(d, z0 .+ d, z0) ≈ 0.0 atol=1e-12
    end

    @testset "reference test" begin
        u, itr_h, res_h = elliptic_1d_dr(; nx=64)
        # the solver converges
        @test res_h[end] < 1e-6
        # the solution matches the reference values from a previous run
        inds  = [8, 16, 32, 48, 56]
        u_ref = [0.12964753561537531, 0.2778162895920091, 0.49914932793046585, 0.70365130873788, 0.8518255710551478]
        @test u[inds] ≈ u_ref rtol=1e-6
    end
end
👉 Run the tests with ] test:(Elliptic1D) pkg> test
     Testing Elliptic1D
...

Test Summary: | Pass  Total  Time
Elliptic1D    |    4      4  1.0s
     Testing Elliptic1D tests passed
Check that the tests detect errors: e.g., change the sign of the flux in the solver, and run the tests again.Testing ParallelStencil codesParallelStencil can only be initialised once per Julia session. To test 2D and 3D codes in the same package, start a separate Julia process for each of them from test/runtests.jl. Base.julia_cmd() returns the command that starts the current Julia executable, and Base.active_project() the project of the test environment.Continuous integration with GitHub ActionsWith continuous integration, the tests run automatically on every push to GitHub. This makes sure that:the tests are always run;failing tests are noticed immediately, e.g. in a pull request, and GitHub notifies you by email.GitHub Actions runs workflows, which are defined in YAML files in the folder .github/workflows of a repository. For example, this course’s website is generated from the lecture files, and deployed by the workflow ExportNotebooks.yml on every push to the course repository.👉 Create the file .github/workflows/CI.yml in the package folder:name: CI

title: Julia MPI
text:
Julia MPIThe goal of this lecture is to become familiar with:Distributed-memory parallelisation: domain decomposition, halo updates and parallel scaling.Fake parallelisation: a proof of concept of the halo update, which runs on a single process.Distributed computing with MPI.jl: a 1D diffusion solver that runs on several processes.In lectures 4–6, we parallelised our solvers on a single CPU with multi-threading, and on a single GPU. In this lecture, we take the next step: we distribute the computations across several processes, each with its own memory, which communicate by exchanging messages.Distributed computingDistributed computing adds one more layer of parallelisation. We need it when the global problem no longer fits on a single compute node or GPU. The resources of a single device, mainly its memory, are finite:on CPUs, distributed computing increases the number of cores beyond what a single CPU, or a single compute node, can offer;on GPUs, it overcomes the limited size of the device memory.Simply put: if one CPU or GPU is not sufficient to solve a problem, use several of them, and solve a part of the global problem on each.Distributed-memory computing lets us take advantage of computing clusters: many similar compute nodes, interconnected by a high-throughput network. Supercomputers, such as Alps, which we use in this course, are clusters of this kind.Parallel scalingLet’s assume that we want to solve a certain problem, which we will call the global problem. We split it into several local problems, which are solved concurrently. There are two approaches to scaling a parallel application to more computing resources: strong scaling and weak scaling.Using more computing resources to solve the same global problem increases parallelism, and may reduce the execution time (wall time). This is called strong scaling: the resources increase, but the size of the global problem doesn’t change, so the global problem is split into more, and smaller, local problems that are solved in parallel.The strong scaling approach is often used when parallelising legacy CPU codes: increasing the number of local problems can lead to some speed-up, up to an optimum beyond which additional processes are no longer beneficial.However, we won’t follow that path when developing multi-GPU applications from scratch. The reason is that the performance of GPUs is very sensitive to the size of the local problem, as we experienced in lecture 5 when tuning the kernel launch parameters, i.e. the numbers of threads and blocks.When developing multi-GPU applications from scratch, it is more suitable to approach distributed parallelism from a weak scaling perspective: first, find the optimal size of the local problem for a single GPU, and then increase the number of local problems, and thus the number of GPUs, until the global problem reaches the size that we originally wanted to solve.Implicit global gridWe can thus replicate a local problem several times in each dimension of the Cartesian space to obtain a global grid, which is therefore defined implicitly. The local problems define each other’s local boundary conditions by exchanging the values at their internal boundaries with inter-process communication, e.g. with the Message Passing Interface (MPI), as depicted in the following figure from ImplicitGlobalGrid.jl:Parallel efficiencyMany things can go wrong in distributed computing. However, our ultimate goal is to maintain a high parallel efficiency.The speed-up \(S\) is the ratio of the execution time on a single processor, \(T_1\), to the execution time on \(n\) processors, \(T_n\). The parallel efficiency \(E\) is the speed-up divided by the number of processors:\[S = \frac{T_1}{T_n}~, \qquad E = \frac{S}{n}~.\]These definitions apply to strong scaling, where the size of the global problem is fixed. We will use the parallel efficiency in a weak scaling configuration, in which the size of the global problem grows proportionally to \(n\). In this case, the ideal execution time stays constant, and the parallel efficiency is \(E = T_1 / T_n\), where \(T_1\) is the execution time of one local problem on one processor, and \(T_n\) the execution time of \(n\) local problems on \(n\) processors.Ideally, the parallel efficiency should stay close to 1 while we increase the number of processors proportionally to the size of the global problem, i.e. at a constant size of the local problems. This means that no time is lost to overheads, e.g. to inter-process communication, network congestion or congestion of the shared file system. The following figure from ImplicitGlobalGrid.jl shows the parallel efficiency of a 3D hydro-mechanical solver, written in CUDA C and in Julia, on up to 5120 GPUs of Piz Daint, the predecessor of Alps at CSCS:Let’s get startedWe will explore distributed computing with MPI.jl, the Julia wrapper of MPI. It enables our codes to run on multiple CPUs and GPUs, and thus to scale on modern multi-CPU and multi-GPU nodes, clusters and supercomputers. In our approach, each MPI process handles one CPU or one GPU.We will tackle distributed parallelisation in three steps:fake parallelisation with 2 fake processes, as a proof of concept;fake parallelisation with np fake processes;a 1D diffusion solver with Julia and MPI.👉 On your computer, create a folder for this lecture, make it a Julia project, and add the packages CairoMakie, JLD2 and MPI.Fake parallelisationAs a first step, we will look at the 1D diffusion solver from lecture 2, parallelised with a “fake parallelisation” approach. We split the computational domain into two parts, the left and the right domain, and store the concentration in two arrays, CL and CR, respectively.In this fake parallelisation, the computations for the left and the right domain are performed sequentially by a single process. However, they could be performed by two distinct processes, if the boundary update, often called halo update in the literature, were done with MPI.The figure shows a global grid made of np = 3 local grids with nx = 6 cells each. The first and the last cell of each local grid are its boundary cells. At the ends of the global domain, they are global boundaries, where the boundary conditions apply. Inside the domain, they are local boundaries, also called halo cells: they hold copies of the values computed by the neighbouring process. Neighbouring local grids thus overlap by 2 cells, and the global grid has nx_g = (nx - 2) * np + 2 cells.The idea of the fake parallelisation is the following:# compute physics locally
qxL         .= .-dc.*diff(CL)./dx
qxR         .= .-dc.*diff(CR)./dx
CL[2:end-1] .-= dt.*diff(qxL)./dx
CR[2:end-1] .-= dt.*diff(qxR)./dx
# update boundaries (MPI)
# CL[end] = ...
# CR[1]   = ...
# global picture
C .= [CL[1:end-1]; CR[2:end]]
Each domain computes its fluxes and updates its inner cells, as the solver of lecture 2 does for the whole domain. The boundary cells CL[end] and CR[1] are not updated: their values must come from the neighbouring domain. A correct boundary update is therefore the critical part of a successful implementation. In our approach, CL and CR overlap by 2 cells, which avoids any wrong computations at the transition between the left and the right domain.Step 1: 2 fake processes👉 Copy the following “fake parallel” 1D diffusion script to a file diffusion_1D_2procs.jl. The script is missing the boundary updates of the 2 fake processes. Run it, and describe what you see in the animation diffusion_1D_2procs.mp4, which the script saves in the current folder.The script also solves the diffusion equation on the global grid, C_g, as a reference, which it plots with markers. At the end, it prints the maximum difference between the solution of the 2 fake processes and the reference.# Linear 1D diffusion with 2 fake MPI processes
using CairoMakie

function diffusion_1D_2procs(; do_visu=true)
    # physics
    lx   = 20.0
    dc   = 1.0
    # numerics
    nx   = 32                 # local number of grid cells
    nvis = 5
    # preprocessing
    nx_g = 2 * (nx - 2) + 2   # global number of grid cells
    dx   = lx / nx_g
    xc_g = LinRange(dx/2, lx-dx/2, nx_g)
    dt   = dx^2 / dc / 2
    nt   = 200
    # array initialisation
    C_g  = @. exp(-(xc_g - lx/2)^2) # global reference
    qx_g = zeros(nx_g-1)
    CL   = C_g[1:nx]                # left local domain
    CR   = C_g[nx-1:end]            # right local domain
    qxL  = zeros(nx-1)
    qxR  = zeros(nx-1)
    C    = [CL[1:end-1]; CR[2:end]] # global picture
    # create plot
    if do_visu
        fig = Figure(size=(600, 300))
        ax  = Axis(fig[1,1]; xlabel="x", ylabel="Concentration")
        ylims!(ax, -0.05, 1.05)
        plt = (scatter!(ax, xc_g, C_g; color=:blue, markersize=6, label="global reference"),
               lines!(ax, xc_g, C; color=:red, linewidth=2, label="2 fake processes"))
        axislegend(ax)
        io  = VideoStream(fig; framerate=10)
    end
    # time loop
    for it = 1:nt
        # compute physics locally
        qxL         .= .-dc.*diff(CL)./dx
        qxR         .= .-dc.*diff(CR)./dx
        CL[2:end-1] .-= dt.*diff(qxL)./dx
        CR[2:end-1] .-= dt.*diff(qxR)./dx
        # update boundaries (MPI)
        # CL[end] = ...
        # CR[1]   = ...
        # global picture
        C .= [CL[1:end-1]; CR[2:end]]
        # compute physics globally (check)
        qx_g         .= .-dc.*diff(C_g)./dx
        C_g[2:end-1] .-= dt.*diff(qx_g)./dx
        # visualisation
        if do_visu && it % nvis == 0
            plt[1][2] = C_g
            plt[2][2] = C
            recordframe!(io)
        end
    end
    println("max. difference to the global reference: ", maximum(abs.(C .- C_g)))
    do_visu && save("diffusion_1D_2procs.mp4", io)
    return
end

diffusion_1D_2procs()
👉 Then, add the required boundary updates to make the code work properly, and run it again. What has changed in the animation?Want to see the answer?AnswerThe last cell of CL overlaps with the second cell of CR, and the first cell of CR overlaps with the second-to-last cell of CL:# update boundaries (MPI)
CL[end] = CR[2]
CR[1]   = CL[end-1]
Without the boundary updates, the overlapping cells CL[end] and CR[1] keep their initial values, and act as fixed boundary conditions in the middle of the domain: the peak of the Gaussian stays at its initial value instead of diffusing. With the boundary updates, the solution of the 2 fake processes matches the global reference, and the script prints a maximum difference of 0:From 2 to np fake processesThe next step is to generalise the fake parallelisation from 2 to np fake processes. The idea of this generalised approach is the following:for ip = 1:np # compute physics locally
    qx[:, ip]      .= .-dc.*diff(C[:, ip])./dx
    C[2:end-1, ip] .-= dt.*diff(qx[:, ip])./dx
end
for ip = 1:np-1 # update boundaries
    # ...
end
The array C now contains np local domains: each column of C belongs to one fake process, namely the process indicated by the second index of C, ip. The boundary updates have to be adapted accordingly. All physical calculations happen on the local chunks of the arrays. We only need “global” knowledge to define the initial condition.Simple initial conditions, e.g. constant values, can be defined without computing any coordinates. To define other initial conditions, such as our Gaussian anomaly, we usually need the global coordinates of the cells. In the code below, the global coordinates of the cell centres can be computed from the process index ip, the cell index ix, the local array size nx, the overlap of the local domains (2 cells) and the grid spacing of the global grid dx. Along the way, we assemble the global coordinates xc_g and the global initial condition C_g, which we use for plotting:# initial condition
for ip = 1:np
    for ix = 1:nx
        # xc[ix, ip] = ...
        C[ix, ip]  = exp(-(xc[ix, ip] - lx/2)^2)
    end

To distribute the computations, we take the following steps:initialise MPI and set up a Cartesian communicator;implement a boundary update routine;create a “global” initial condition;finalise MPI.1. Initialising MPITo initialise MPI and to set up the Cartesian communicator, we write:import MPI

MPI.Init()
comm        = MPI.COMM_WORLD
nprocs      = MPI.Comm_size(comm)
dims        = MPI.Dims_create(nprocs, [0])
comm_cart   = MPI.Cart_create(comm, dims)
me          = MPI.Comm_rank(comm_cart)
coords      = MPI.Cart_coords(comm_cart)
neighbors_x = MPI.Cart_shift(comm_cart, 0, 1)
The communicator MPI.COMM_WORLD contains all MPI processes, and MPI.Comm_size returns their number, nprocs.MPI.Dims_create distributes the processes over the dimensions of a Cartesian grid of processes. The zeros mark the dimensions in which MPI is free to choose the number of processes: in 1D, dims = [nprocs].MPI.Cart_create creates a new communicator, comm_cart, in which the processes are arranged on this Cartesian grid. By default, the grid is not periodic.me is the rank of the process, a unique ID of each MPI process, starting at 0. It is the analogue of ip in the fake parallelisation.coords contains the coordinates of the process in the grid of processes, also starting at 0.MPI.Cart_shift returns the ranks of the left and the right neighbour, neighbors_x[1] and neighbors_x[2]. At the ends of the global domain, a process has no neighbour on one side, and the corresponding rank is MPI.PROC_NULL.2. Boundary update routineThen, we implement a boundary update routine, which can have the following structure:function update_halo!(A, neighbors_x, comm)
    # send to / receive from neighbour 1 ("left neighbour")
    if neighbors_x[1] != MPI.PROC_NULL
        sendbuf = ??
        recvbuf = ??
        MPI.Send(??, comm; dest=neighbors_x[?], tag=0)
        MPI.Recv!(??, comm; source=neighbors_x[?], tag=1)
        A[1] = ??
    end
    # send to / receive from neighbour 2 ("right neighbour")
    if neighbors_x[2] != MPI.PROC_NULL
        sendbuf = ??
        recvbuf = ??
        MPI.Recv!(??, comm; source=neighbors_x[?], tag=0)
        MPI.Send(??, comm; dest=neighbors_x[?], tag=1)
        A[end] = ??
    end
    return
end
MPI.Send sends the data in a buffer to the process with the rank dest, and MPI.Recv! receives data from the process with the rank source into a pre-allocated buffer. The tag identifies the message: each MPI.Send is matched by an MPI.Recv! with the same tag on the receiving process.Blocking communicationMPI.Send and MPI.Recv! are blocking: MPI.Recv! returns only once the message has been received, and MPI.Send may wait until the receiving process is ready. Therefore, the order of the calls matters. Every process first exchanges data with its left neighbour, sending first, and then with its right neighbour, receiving first. This way, the MPI.Send of a process to its left neighbour always meets the MPI.Recv! of that neighbour from its right neighbour. If both processes started with MPI.Send, they could wait for each other forever, which is called a deadlock.3. function diffusion_1D_mpi(; do_save=false)
    # MPI
    MPI.Init()
    comm        = MPI.COMM_WORLD
    nprocs      = MPI.Comm_size(comm)
    dims        = MPI.Dims_create(nprocs, [0])
    comm_cart   = MPI.Cart_create(comm, dims)
    me          = MPI.Comm_rank(comm_cart)
    coords      = MPI.Cart_coords(comm_cart)
    neighbors_x = MPI.Cart_shift(comm_cart, 0, 1)
    if (me == 0) println("nprocs = $(nprocs), dims[1] = $(dims[1])") end
    # physics
    lx   = 20.0
    dc   = 1.0
    # numerics
    nx   = 32                     # local number of grid cells
    # preprocessing
    nx_g = dims[1] * (nx - 2) + 2 # global number of grid cells
    dx   = lx / nx_g
    dt   = dx^2 / dc / 2
    nt   = 100
    # array initialisation
    x0   = coords[1] * (nx - 2) * dx
    xc   = [x0 + ix*dx - dx/2 for ix = 1:nx]
    C    = @. exp(-(xc - lx/2)^2)
    qx   = zeros(nx-1)
    # time loop
    t_tic = 0.0
    for it = 1:nt
        # start the timer after 10 warm-up iterations
        if (it == 11) t_tic = Base.time() end
        qx         .= .-dc.*diff(C)./dx
        C[2:end-1] .-= dt.*diff(qx)./dx
        update_halo!(C, neighbors_x, comm_cart)
    end
    # performance
    t_toc = Base.time() - t_tic
    t_it  = t_toc / (nt - 10)              # execution time per iteration [s]
    A_eff = 2 * nx * sizeof(Float64) / 1e9 # effective main memory access per iteration [GB]
    T_eff = A_eff / t_it                   # effective memory throughput [GB/s]
    if (me == 0) @printf("Time = %1.3e s, T_eff = %1.2f GB/s\n", t_toc, T_eff) end
    # save the local arrays for visualisation
    if do_save
        jldsave(joinpath(@__DIR__, "mpi1D_out_$(me).jld2"); C, xc)
    end
    MPI.Finalize()
    return
end
